guide.title: Sallustiano, Rome: rione XVII, Bernini's Saint Teresa and the Gardens of Sallust
guide.intro: Sallustiano is rione XVII of Rome, Roma Capitale's toponymic code 117. Roma Capitale's Annuario statistico 2022 gives it 0,2 km² and 2.191 residents at 31 December 2021. It was created in 1921, one of seven rioni instituted by the Giunta Municipale and each given a coat of arms. Italian Wikipedia describes it as two zones — a reasonably residential strip between via Piave and via Piemonte/via Salandra, and the rest, down to via Bissolati, «praticamente disabitata e con un'alta concentrazione di uffici e ministeri», practically uninhabited and thick with offices and ministries. That is the honest shape of the place. What brings a traveller here is one chapel: Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, in Santa Maria della Vittoria. Around it are the sunken Gardens of Sallust, two more churches, a state museum of fashion and decorative arts, and a street of turn-of-the-century villini, most of them now offices.

sections.heading: What the rione is, and where its edges run
sections.body:
Italian Wikipedia gives the rione's arms as a gold mirror of Venus Erycina on blue — «Di azzurro allo specchio di Venere Ericina d'oro» — alluding to the goddess's temple in the Gardens of Sallust, citing Carlo Pietrangeli's 1953 article on the arms of the rioni of Rome.

The same article states the borders in one sentence: «Mura aureliane fino a piazza Fiume (esclusa) con il quartiere Salario; via Calabria-via Boncompagni-via Lucullo-via Friuli con il rione Ludovisi; via Leonida Bissolati-largo Santa Susanna con Trevi e via XX Settembre fino a Porta Pia (esclusa) con il rione Castro Pretorio.» In English: the Aurelian Walls as far as piazza Fiume, which is excluded, with the quartiere Salario; via Calabria–via Boncompagni–via Lucullo–via Friuli with the rione Ludovisi; via Leonida Bissolati–largo di Santa Susanna with Trevi; and via XX Settembre as far as Porta Pia, which is excluded, with the rione Castro Pretorio. The Ludovisi article describes the same staircase of streets in reverse, so the two rioni carved out of one estate do not in fact disagree about where the line runs. Two consequences are worth carrying in your head: Porta Pia is outside this rione, and so is piazza Fiume.

The history, as Italian Wikipedia tells it: this was part of the Augustan Regio VI Alta Semita; the Horti Sallustiani and a temple of Venus Erycina stood here; via Piave follows the line of the via Salaria Nova running out of the former Porta Collina toward the demolished Porta Salaria. Alaric's Visigoths cut the aqueducts and sacked Sallust's villa in 410, after which the ground between the Pincio and the Quirinal emptied out. There was a partial revival in the sixteenth century with the opening of via Pia and Sixtus V's Acqua Felice, but the zone stayed thinly populated and formed part of the rione Trevi, holding large villas — villa Barberini, villa Mandosi, villa Cicciaporci. It was built up after 1870 and constituted as its own rione in 1921. Via XX Settembre itself is the ancient Alta Semita line, opened in the sixteenth century as via Pia and renamed for the date of the 1870 breach; it is context here and not a place in this corpus, because it is filed under three different rioni by its own sources.

Italian Wikipedia states that a surviving green space of the rione is the ground against the walls between Porta Pia, via Augusto Valenziani and via Piave — the grounds of the former villa Cicciaporci Valenti Gonzaga, now known as villa Paolina. It is inside an embassy compound and you cannot walk in it.

Sallustiano falls in Municipio I. No source states the heritage protection status of any building in the rione, so nothing here says a building is protected.

sections.heading: Villini, ministries and embassies
sections.body:
The plots north of via Boncompagni were subdivided out of the Villa Ludovisi estate from 1883 and built up as detached villini around the turn of the twentieth century. Italian Wikipedia records villino Rattazzi at via Boncompagni 8–10, of about 1900, by Giulio Podesti for the family of Urbano Rattazzi, third prime minister of the Kingdom of Italy; villino Pignatelli at no. 12, of 1898, by Giuseppe Mariani for Duke Giuseppe di Terranova Pignatelli; villino Rasponi at no. 14, of 1901, by Carlo Pincherle, the father of Alberto Moravia, for Count Giulio Rasponi Murat; villino Levi at no. 28 on the corner of via Nerva, of about 1890, by Augusto Giustini for Baron Giorgio Levi delle Trezze and enlarged in 1905 by Pincherle; villino Casati at via Piemonte 51, of 1906, built by Pincherle to a design by Achille Majnoni d'Intignano for the Casati Stampa di Soncino and the Roman residence of the Marchesa Luisa Casati; and villino Maccari on via Sallustiana, of 1902, by Augusto Fallani for the painter Cesare Maccari. Most are now offices, and none is open to visitors. Italian Wikipedia cites no sources for the Pignatelli, Rasponi and Levi articles.

Two larger buildings belong to the same passage. Italian Wikipedia records Palazzo Fiat on via Calabria, of 1924–26, in the barocchetto manner, by Enrico Del Debbio; and the Palazzo della Società Beni Stabili on via Piemonte at the corner of via Giosuè Carducci, of 1957, modernist, by the engineer Cesare Pascoletti. Neither is a visitor place either.

Note that via Boncompagni, via Calabria, via Lucullo and via Friuli are the declared line between Sallustiano and Ludovisi. Buildings on them can sit on either side, and this guide claims buildings rather than streets.

The rest of the rione is government and diplomacy. Alongside the Ministry of Agriculture on via XX Settembre and the Ministero dell'ambiente e della sicurezza energetica at via Sallustiana 53, boundary tests put a cluster of diplomatic missions inside these few blocks: the Embassy of France to the Holy See at Villa Paolina on via Piave, the chancery and consular section of the Embassy of Japan to the Italian State in the villino Rudinì on via Quintino Sella, the Embassy of Eritrea on via Boncompagni, and the embassies of Cape Verde and of Timor-Leste to the Holy See on via Giosuè Carducci. None of them is a visitor place, and one point matters more than any of them individually: a diplomatic mission stands on the territory of the state that hosts it. Every one of these buildings is on Italian soil in the rione Sallustiano. None is foreign territory, none is Vatican territory, and none is one of the Lateran Treaty's extraterritorial properties — an embassy accredited to the Holy See is not in the Vatican, it is on via Piave.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
Sallustiano is 0,2 km² of Rome between the Aurelian Walls and via Leonida Bissolati. If you are trying to find it on the ground, use the four edges the rione's own description gives: the walls down to piazza Fiume, which is outside it; via Calabria, via Boncompagni, via Lucullo and via Friuli on the Ludovisi side; via Leonida Bissolati and largo di Santa Susanna on the Trevi side; and via XX Settembre as far as Porta Pia, which is outside it, on the Castro Pretorio side. Santa Maria della Vittoria stands on the north side of via XX Settembre, at the corner of largo di Santa Susanna, and is the easiest fixed point in the rione.

For public transport, the only measured distance published by any source this guide fetched is the one on the Horti Sallustiani venue's own website, which gives under Come raggiungerci «Fermata Metro A Barberini-Repubblica, 800 mt» — metro line A at Barberini–Repubblica, 800 metres. No bus route numbers are given here, because none was sourced. The same page also gives a walking time, which this guide does not repeat: walking times are not something a guide can check for you.

One thing this guide will not do is tell you how long anything takes or how close anything feels. Where a distance is stated it is a measured figure from the source named beside it.

faq.question: Where is Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa, and when can I see it?
faq.answer: In the Cornaro Chapel of Santa Maria della Vittoria, Via XX Settembre 17, 00187 Roma. The Discalced Carmelite province of central Italy, whose community serves the church, publishes these hours: the church open 6.45–12.00 and 16.00–19.00, and on Sundays 9.00–12.00 and 16.00–18.00. Visiting hours are given separately as 8.00–12.00 and 16.00–18.00 on weekdays and 9.00–12.00 and 16.00–18.00 on Sundays. The same page states that visits are not permitted during services and asks guided groups to use audio headsets. Hours as published by the province and checked on 2 September 2026.

faq.question: Can I go inside the Gardens of Sallust?
faq.answer: Not on a walk-in basis. The Aula is run as a private venue for hire. Its own website advertises corporate events, conferences and meetings, receptions, gala dinners, fashion shows, art exhibitions, music events and photographic and film shoots, and offers an enquiry form rather than opening hours; no public opening hours and no admission price are published. Enquiries: 06 4201 1597, or eventi@hortisallustiani.it. The remains themselves lie 14 metres below street level and Italian Wikipedia says they can still be seen in piazza Sallustio.

faq.question: Is Villa Bonaparte open to visitors, and is it French territory?
faq.answer: It is not open, and it is not French territory. Villa Paolina, also called Villa Bonaparte, is the seat of the Embassy of France to the Holy See, with its entrance on via Piave. It is a diplomatic mission standing on Italian soil in the rione Sallustiano: it is not Vatican territory, it is not French territory, and it is not one of the Lateran Treaty's extraterritorial properties. No source fetched for this guide gives any public opening, and the garden inside the compound is not a public park.

faq.question: What are the Museo Boncompagni Ludovisi's opening hours and admission?
faq.answer: No sourced opening hours or admission price are given here. Italian Wikipedia states hours and prices for the museum but cites no source for them; they are not repeated. The address is Via Boncompagni 18.

faq.question: Is Porta Pia in Sallustiano?
faq.answer: No. The rione's own border description runs along via XX Settembre «fino a Porta Pia (esclusa)» — as far as Porta Pia, excluded — and boundary tests put the gate outside this rione. Porta Pia belongs to the rione Castro Pretorio. Sallustiano does touch the Aurelian Walls, but this guide names no stretch of the walls as a place of its own: the wall line is a boundary here, and a boundary is not a place inside the thing it bounds.

faq.question: Santa Maria della Vittoria and Santa Susanna face each other. Are both in this rione?
faq.answer: No. Santa Maria della Vittoria is in Sallustiano — boundary tests put both the church building and Roma Capitale's own published point for it inside the rione, and it stands on the north side of via XX Settembre. Santa Susanna is not in Sallustiano, and this guide does not state which rione it is in, because the sources that were checked do not agree. Largo di Santa Susanna itself is not claimed here either: Italian Wikipedia says the square lies partly in Sallustiano and partly in Trevi.

photos.title: Santa Maria della Vittoria
photos.description: The travertine facade of Santa Maria della Vittoria on via XX Settembre, built in 1626 to Giovan Battista Soria's design at the expense of Cardinal Scipione Borghese, whose dedication is cut into the entablature.
photos.author: Diego Delso

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Vittoria
places.summary: A seventeenth-century Carmelite church on the north side of via XX Settembre, at the corner of largo di Santa Susanna, holding Bernini's Ecstasy of Saint Teresa of Ávila in the Cornaro Chapel.
places.history:
Roma Capitale's tourism portal gives the history. The church was designed by Carlo Maderno and built between 1608 and 1620, first as a chapel dedicated to St Paul for the Discalced Carmelites. Its present title comes from the Catholic army's victory over the Bohemians at the battle of the White Mountain near Prague on 8 November 1620; the miraculous image was carried into the church on 8 May 1622. The travertine façade went up in 1626 to Giovan Battista Soria's design, at the expense of Cardinal Scipione Borghese, in exchange for the Sleeping Hermaphrodite found in 1608 during the digging of the church's foundations. Inside it is a Latin cross with a single nave, a barrel vault and three chapels a side; the vault and dome were painted by Giandomenico Cerrini and the apse by Luigi Serra, and there are works by Guercino, Nicolas Lorrain and Domenichino.

The Cornaro Chapel was commissioned from Gian Lorenzo Bernini by the family of Cardinal Federico Cornaro. The Ecstasy of Saint Teresa of Ávila is in marble and gilt bronze and was executed between 1647 and 1652; members of the Cornaro family watch the scene from what read as theatre boxes. The Carmelite province's site carries a notice dated 22 October 2021 announcing the inauguration of the Cornaro Chapel after its restoration, which the same page attributes to the Soprintendenza Speciale di Roma.

The Discalced Carmelite province of central Italy, whose community serves the church, publishes these hours: the church open 6.45–12.00 and 16.00–19.00, and on Sundays 9.00–12.00 and 16.00–18.00. Visiting hours are given separately as 8.00–12.00 and 16.00–18.00 on weekdays and 9.00–12.00 and 16.00–18.00 on Sundays. Mass is at 7.00 Monday to Saturday and 10.30 on Sundays and holy days of obligation; Eucharistic adoration is on Tuesdays 18.00–19.00 and Thursdays 18.30–19.00. The same page states that visits are not permitted during services and asks guided groups to use audio headsets. Hours as published by the province and checked on 2 September 2026. Contacts, from Roma Capitale: tel. 06 42740571, vittoria@carmelitaniroma.it.

Roma Capitale's page also links the Holy See's Jubilee 2025 site, which places the church on one of the jubilee walking routes inside Rome. That page is cited here for the routing and for nothing else: its opening history describes a different church of the same name, in Mantua, and no history has been taken from it.

places.name: Horti Sallustiani — Aula Adrianea
places.summary: The surviving core of the Gardens of Sallust, 14 metres below the modern street in piazza Sallustio, and the source of the rione's name. Roma Capitale's tourism portal calls the Horti Sallustiani, with their gardens and villa, a monumental park covering the ground between today's via Salaria, via Veneto, via XX Settembre and the Aurelian Walls.
places.history:
The address is Piazza Sallustio 21, 00187 Rome — the address given both by Roma Capitale's tourism portal and on the site's own website. Italian Wikipedia calls piazza Sallustio a square of the rione, and the centre of it, with the remains of the Horti Sallustiani from which the rione takes its name still visible there.

Roma Capitale's account: the land had been Julius Caesar's and was bought by the historian Sallust in 44 BC. It passed into imperial ownership under Tiberius; Vespasian liked to stay there and Nerva died there; there was further work under Hadrian and under Aurelian, who added a hippodrome he rode in. The gardens were badly damaged in the invasion of 410 and never rebuilt.

What survives at piazza Sallustio, 14 metres below street level, is a three-part complex. The principal element is a large circular domed hall, which the portal compares to the Serapeum of Hadrian's Villa, with niches in its walls, two of them opening into side rooms that may have been nymphaea; a glazed opening in the modern cocciopesto floor lets you look down at the hall's foundation. Behind it stands a semicircular multi-storey residential building with frescoed rooms, mosaic floors and windows, and a wide north stair once led to upper floors that have vanished. In 1998 the Soprintendenza approved a recovery project for the Aula Adrianea, to bring it back into use for cultural events and conferences.

Access, which is the question everybody asks: the Aula is run as a private venue for hire. Its own website advertises corporate events, conferences and meetings, receptions, gala dinners, fashion shows, art exhibitions, music events and photographic and film shoots, and offers an enquiry form rather than opening hours; no public opening hours and no admission price are published. Enquiries: 06 4201 1597, or eventi@hortisallustiani.it. The site's footer carries the copyright of Tecno Holding S.p.A. One warning worth carrying: the venue's site is hortisallustiani.it, without a hyphen. The hyphenated horti-sallustiani.it is a parked domain offered for sale, and it is what OpenStreetMap has tagged as the site's website. Do not cite the hyphenated domain as the venue's official site.

Provenance, from the same Roma Capitale page, and provenance only: the Dying Gaul, the Suicidal Gaul, the Ludovisi Throne and the obelisk that now stands above the Spanish Steps all came out of the Horti. None of them is in Sallustiano today, and none of the museums that hold them is written up in this guide.

places.name: Museo Boncompagni Ludovisi per le arti decorative
places.summary: A state museum of decorative arts, costume and Italian fashion, in the villino the Boncompagni Ludovisi princes built for themselves on via Boncompagni. It is the place where the family name on the street signs stops being an abstraction.
places.history:
Italian Wikipedia gives the museum's full name as the Museo Andrea e Blanceflor Boncompagni Ludovisi, dedicated to decorative arts, costume and Italian fashion and housed in the Villino Boncompagni Ludovisi. The building was left to the Italian State in 1972 by the will of Princess Blanceflor de Bildt Boncompagni, to be kept and used "esclusivamente per scopi artistico-culturali di pubblica utilità", and it opened to the public in 1995. Administratively it is state-owned, formerly under the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna, from December 2014 under the Polo museale del Lazio and from December 2019 under the Direzione Musei statali di Roma. The same article records 9.782 visitors in 2018, citing a MiBAC spreadsheet.

Italian Wikipedia describes five exhibition rooms holding the villino's original furnishings — furniture, tapestries, paintings and ceramics — alongside a collection covering Italian fashion, costume and design, with garments by Fausto Sarli, Fernanda Gattinoni, Valentino, Roberto Capucci, Raffaella Curiel, Lorenzo Riva, Renato Balestra, Mila Schön, André Laug and Angelo Litrico, and a group of dresses that belonged to Palma Bucarelli, director of the Galleria nazionale d'arte moderna from 1941 to 1975, added in 1996.

No sourced opening hours or admission price are given here. Italian Wikipedia states hours and prices for the museum but cites no source for them; they are not repeated. Check before travelling.

The building, according to Italian Wikipedia, which cites no source — the article carries the encyclopedia's own unsourced banner, dated November 2015 — was built in 1901–1903 by the architect Giovanni Battista Giovenale (1849–1934) for the Boncompagni Ludovisi princes, on a plot at the corner of via Boncompagni and via Quintino Sella that had been part of Villa Ludovisi and was subdivided from 1883. It has two storeys over a basement and mezzanine, crowned by a balustrade; the short side faces via Boncompagni and the other three façades face the garden; the manner is a sober barocchetto with rococo flourishes in the window frames and in the via Boncompagni portal.

A wording trap worth knowing about, because it will confuse you if you read around: that article's lead sentence places the villino in "Rione XVII Sallustiano, quartiere Ludovisi". The first is the rione, which is this one; the second is the neighbourhood-sense Ludovisi district, which is a different thing from the rione Ludovisi. The museum is in Sallustiano.

places.name: Basilica di San Camillo de Lellis
places.summary: A brick and travertine parish church of the early twentieth century, neo-Romanesque with Gothic inflections, built for the order Camillus de Lellis founded and raised to minor basilica in 1965. Its campanile, at 30 metres, is the marker for this end of the rione.
places.history:
Roma Capitale's tourism portal gives the account. The church was built at the wish of Pope Pius X to a design by the architect Tullio Passarelli; construction began in 1906 and the first stone was laid by Cardinal Antonio Agliardi; it was consecrated and erected as a parish in 1910 and entrusted to the Clerks Regular Ministers of the Infirm, the order founded by Camillus de Lellis. In 1965 Paul VI raised it to minor basilica and created the cardinalatial title San Camillo de Lellis agli Orti Sallustiani.

The outside is red brick with stone detail and the inside is travertine block throughout, on a Latin cross plan. Three portals stand under lunette reliefs, with Christ presents St Camillus to the sick in the centre, beneath a large rose window; a 1907 relief of Christ the Good Shepherd is set over the side portal on via Sallustiana. The square campanile carries a pyramidal spire and reaches 30 metres. Inside there are three aisles on round arches under cross vaults, five apse windows showing Christ and the four Evangelists, and a statue of St Camillus by Alberto Galli of 1911. The organ was built in 1910–11 by Carlo Vegezzi-Bossi, opus 1314, to Filippo Capocci's design and was donated by Margherita of Savoy; electric action was installed in 1999 in place of the original pneumatic action, and it has 29 stops over two manuals and pedal.

Roma Capitale's tourism portal publishes the parish's mass times. In autumn and winter: Monday to Saturday 09.00 and 18.00; Sundays and feasts 09.00, 11.30 and 19.00. In spring and summer: Monday to Saturday 09.00 and 19.00; Sundays and feasts 09.00, 11.30 and 19.00. The portal itself warns that times may change and that changes are posted on the church's external noticeboards. As published by the portal and checked on 2 September 2026. Tel. 06 4818188.

According to Italian Wikipedia, the church stands on the site of the former villa Spithöver, a neo-Renaissance building of 1870 by Luca Carimini, demolished at the end of the nineteenth century; the church itself went up between 1906 and 1910.

places.name: Chiesa del Sacro Cuore di Gesù
places.summary: A church of 1914–1916 by Aristide Leonori on via Piave, set back behind a wrought-iron railing with a five-arched loggia across the front. Its Munich glass and the tomb of the foundress of the congregation that runs it are the reasons to look inside; the address is the street only, because no street number could be sourced.
places.history:
Via Piave. No street number could be sourced.

Italian Wikipedia's account: the church was built between 1914 and 1916 to a design by Aristide Leonori. Its elevation gives onto via Piave, although the original project faced it to via XX Settembre, and it is separated from the street by a wrought-iron railing. The façade is fronted by a central projecting body with a five-arched loggia reached by two side ramps. Inside are three aisles on columns carrying a matroneum under an ogival vault; the windows above the matroneum are glazed with glass from Munich showing saints whose names match those of the architect's family. The transept windows show the Institution of the Eucharist and the Sacrifice of Melchizedek on the right; the left transept window is described by Italian Wikipedia as an Adoration of the Eucharist by all the peoples of the world («Adorazione dell'Eucaristia da parte di tutte le razze»). The side apses hold a St Ignatius of Loyola and a copy of the Madonna della Strada, and the central apse is in marble and mosaic with Christ among saints.

The church is run by the Ancelle del Sacro Cuore di Gesù, the Handmaids of the Sacred Heart, of Madrid, and the same article says the congregation's convent adjoins the church. Italian Wikipedia states that the body of the congregation's foundress, Rafaela Porras y Ayllón, lies in a chapel on the left-hand side of the church.

No opening hours and no mass times are given here: none was found in any source fetched for this guide. The article's own lead places the church «situato nel rione Sallustiano, in via Piave», which is the cleanest rione attribution of any building on this page. The aggregator Roma Segreta also indexes the church under Sallustiano.

places.name: Villa Paolina Bonaparte
places.summary: An eighteenth-century casino in its own park against the Aurelian Walls, lived in by Napoleon's sister and now the Embassy of France to the Holy See. You cannot go in; what you can do is understand why the orange trees on via XX Settembre are there.
places.history:
Villa Paolina, also called Villa Bonaparte, is the seat of the Embassy of France to the Holy See, with its entrance on via Piave. It is a diplomatic mission standing on Italian soil in the rione Sallustiano: it is not Vatican territory, it is not French territory, and it is not one of the Lateran Treaty's extraterritorial properties. Roma Capitale's tourism portal states the embassy identity itself.

The same portal gives the history. What stands here is what survives of a villa that ran inside the Aurelian Walls between Porta Pia and Porta Salaria, with the casino in the middle of the park. It was built in 1750 for Cardinal Silvio Valenti Gonzaga, Secretary of State to Benedict XIV, who turned orchards into gardens with exotic planting and raised the villino at their centre. Roma Capitale's tourism portal states that Paolina Borghese, Napoleon's sister, bought the villa in 1816 and lived there until 1824; the same page's historical note says she reached Rome in 1815 and bought Villa Valenti then. On her death in 1825 it passed to her nephews and their descendants.

They held it until 1906, when it was sold to the Prussian government, which installed its legation to the Holy See in 1908 and the German embassy from 1920 to 1944. Reich property was taken by the Allies in 1945; France acquired the villa, and on 15 December 1950 Wladimir d'Ormesson moved the French embassy to the Holy See into Villa Bonaparte. That date is Roma Capitale's; Italian Wikipedia dates the French embassy's arrival to 1951, and the discrepancy is left standing rather than resolved.

Roma Capitale's tourism portal states that it was inside Villa Paolina that the bersaglieri found themselves when they got through the Aurelian Walls at the breach of Porta Pia in 1870. The same page offers a detail you can check on foot: the orange trees planted along the pavement of via XX Settembre opposite the Ministry of the Treasury are a memento of the villa's orangery.

The villa is not visitable and no source fetched for this guide gives any public opening. The garden inside the compound is not a public park and is not written here as one. One caution for anyone searching: it.ambafrance.org is the French embassy to Italy, a different mission, and is not this building's website.

places.name: Palazzo dell'Agricoltura
places.summary: The seat of the Italian agriculture ministry, built 1908–1914, with a frieze of Latin inscriptions outside and an atrium of twenty-two red granite columns inside. It is a working ministry and you cannot walk in, but it is the building that explains what most of this rione is for.
places.history:
Italian Wikipedia records that the palazzo was built between 1908 and 1914 at the wish of Francesco Cocco-Ortu, Minister of Agriculture, Industry and Commerce. The frieze carries three Latin inscriptions, and the interior decoration runs on agricultural and rural themes, with the article's own caveat that the documentation is too thin to explain how the artists were chosen. The building houses the biblioteca storica nazionale dell'agricoltura, first created in 1848, and it is the seat of the Ministero dell'agricoltura, della sovranità alimentare e delle foreste.

The Ministry's own account of the building describes an atrium by the engineer Giuseppe Canonica, who found the original vestibule too cramped, had its end wall taken down and moved the columns so that they became load-bearing. It has twenty-two columns of red Baveno granite and bronze high reliefs above its six side doors, framed in coloured marble. The five gates connecting the atrium to the street, the lamps outside and the wrought-iron lights within are by the Roman artist Alberto Gerardi, who won the competition held for the commission. Three bronze bas-reliefs on the left-hand wall are by the Sicilian sculptor Benedetto D'Amore — the Ploughing, the Wheat Harvest and the Working of Iron — and three on the right, on the theme of human labour, are by Guido Calori.

The building is a working ministry and is not open to callers; the Ministry publishes a virtual tour of it instead.

places.name: Villino Rudinì
places.summary: Ernesto Basile's villino of 1904–1906 for a former prime minister's family: a severe block set back from the street, with Liberty ornament worked into the frieze, the window frames, the railings and the gate. It now holds a diplomatic chancery and is not open to visitors.
places.history:
Italian Wikipedia records that the villino was designed and built between 1904 and 1906 by Ernesto Basile for the family of Antonio Starabba, marchese di Rudinì, twice Prime Minister of the Kingdom of Italy. It is a severe parallelepiped set back from the street, three storeys over a basement plus a recessed attic, entered through a projecting body of three round arches. The shell is post-Risorgimento and monumental in manner, and the decoration is Liberty: squared mullioned windows in the attic, a frieze running the full perimeter, and floral Art Nouveau motifs in the window frames, the portico, the railings and the gate.

The same article, citing L'Architettura Italiana of December 1907, names the craftsmen: the Palermo sculptor Gaetano Geraci executed the principal ornamental sculpture, the stuccoist G. Varnesi of Rome the secondary work, the Li Vigni firm the front portico and hall decoration, and Antonio Ronconi the wrought iron.

Italian Wikipedia states that the villino houses the chancery and consular section of the Embassy of Japan to the Italian State. Diplomatic premises stand on Italian soil; the building is not Japanese territory. It is not open to visitors.

places.name: Palazzo Canevari
places.address: Largo di Santa Susanna 13, Roma RM
places.summary: Built 1873–1881 to house the Kingdom of Italy's geological survey and its museum, and closed since 1995. You cannot go inside; it is here because Roma Capitale still publishes an account of it.
places.history:
Roma Capitale's tourism portal records that the palazzo was wanted by Quintino Sella to house the Regio Ufficio Geologico and its Museo Agrario-Geologico, and was built between 1873 and 1881 to the design of the engineer Raffaele Canevari. Canevari reused seventeenth-century masonry and built exhibition rooms carried on cast-iron piers, with a gallery over a large reading room. It was inaugurated on 3 May 1885 in the presence of King Umberto I. Roma Capitale's tourism portal describes the palazzo as considered among the first examples of 'stile liberty' in Italian public building.

It housed the Geological Institute and the museum collections until 1995, when it was closed. There is no public access. According to Italian Wikipedia's infobox, which cites nothing, the building is under refurbishment and is owned by Cassa depositi e prestiti.

On the address: Roma Capitale publishes it as Largo di Santa Susanna 13, and Italian Wikipedia says that square lies partly in the rione Sallustiano and partly in Trevi. This guide claims the building, which boundary tests put inside Sallustiano, and not the square, which is claimed here for no rione at all.

links.note: Ludovisi and Sallustiano were carved from the same Villa Ludovisi estate. Via Calabria, via Boncompagni, via Lucullo and via Friuli are the line between them.
Via XX Settembre is the border between the two rioni, and Sallustiano's own boundary text runs along it as far as Porta Pia, which is Castro Pretorio's.
Prati is rione XXII in Roma Capitale's toponymic list of Rome's 22 rioni; Sallustiano is rione XVII.
